did_you_know.text: The verb “yinnazeru” comes from the root נ־ז־ר, meaning “to separate” or “to withdraw.” Here it means that priests must stay away from sacred food when they are not permitted to eat it.
The phrase “the soul shall be cut off” is a biblical formula for a serious punishment by Heaven. The Sages and later commentators differed over its exact meaning.
In the purity laws of this chapter, sunset marks the end of the day and the transition to a new state of purity. Purification therefore depends not only on washing, but also on time.

The word “zar” here does not necessarily mean a non-Israelite; it can mean someone outside the priestly family or priestly role. Even a hired worker in a priest’s household does not automatically share the family’s privileges.

“A fifth of it” means adding one-fifth of the sacred item’s value, beyond returning the item itself. This shows that an accidental misuse of sacred property required both correction and financial responsibility.
The word “tamim” here describes an animal without a physical defect, not a person with moral perfection. “Lirtzonkhem” means that the offering will be accepted favorably by God.

The chapter distinguishes between a vow and a voluntary gift: an animal with an unusual form may be given voluntarily, but it cannot fulfill a vow. This shows that vows had a particularly binding status.
A newborn animal does not become eligible for sacrifice immediately; the Torah assigns it a waiting period of seven days. This distinguishes the moment of birth from its qualification for sacred use.

The later Jewish legal tradition calls the prohibition against slaughtering a mother and its offspring on the same day “oto ve’et beno.” It applies to cattle and sheep and is often understood as expressing sensitivity toward the bond between mother and offspring.

The thanksgiving offering was a type of peace offering, and chapter 7 says it was brought with several kinds of bread. It therefore combined gratitude to God with a shared meal for the offerer and others.

The Jewish concept of “kiddush hashem,” honoring God’s name through one’s life and actions, developed from the phrase “I shall be sanctified.” It is the counterpart and opposite of “hillul hashem,” desecrating God’s name.
